newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols bid as spot pokes 1.76.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols bid as spot pokes 1.76.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/mark options rose grudgingly in U.S. business as the spot greenback poked at fresh 41-month highs just above 1.76 marks, dealers said.

Dollar/mark volatilities in the past week had shown only lukewarm response to the dollar's almost daily advances to new highs, but some traders saw bids for options returning as short positions in upside strikes were getting more exposed.
"It's not a lot, but it (volatility) is the highest in days," a trader at a U.S. bank in the West Coast said of the mild gains in volatility levels today.
He said a clear break in spot above 1.76 marks could usher in a wave of option short-covering.
One-month dollar/mark implied volatility stood at 8.2/8.5 percent at U.S. midsession, up about a quarter point on the day, as the dollar hovered at around 1.76 marks.
"It was hard to kick down the one-month any further," an interbank options broker in New York said, noting that the market was starting to see value in volatilities.
He added that a lot of one-month options traded at the 8.35 percent level and that there was also strong interest for overnight options.
Still, on the whole traders agreed that bids have been fairly moderate.

"The dollar has been moving in the direction that everyone anticipated, and a lot of people who need options as protection already have upside strikes," said Kyoko Hiramatsu, a senior dealer at Bank of Yokohama in New York.
The market was probably less prepared to see a sharp downturn in the dollar, she added.
Despite the dollar's steady gains, risk reversals -- the put/call pricing differential -- showed very little preference for upside strikes.
One-month 25-delta was pegged at par to 0.2 percentage point in favor of mark puts.

By contrast, dollar/yen risk reversals remained sharply skewed in favor of downside strikes. One-month 25-delta was at 2.7/3.0 points bid for yen calls. Until a few months ago, a skew of 1.0 point would have been considered steep.
"You could say it's a bit overdone, but evidently some people still need those downside strikes," Hiramatsu said.
Traders said end-user demand for low-delta yen calls remained robust and that many dealers who had sold those options to customers were still on their toes.
The interbank broker said Japanese corporations bought deep out-of-the-money yen calls, in the 10-15 delta range, in the Tokyo market overnight.
Dollar/yen volatilities were generally softer. One-month was off about 0.4 point from Monday at 12.0/12.3 percent.

The West Coast trader noted that volatilities were slow to recoil when the dollar clawed back above 113 yen overnight in response to dollar-supportive remarks by the Japanese Finance Ministry's forex guru Eisuke Sakakibara, who said the ministry had no intention of using exchange rates as an instrument of trade policy.
-- Chicago Derivatives Desk ((312-408-8750))
